1943.label: Player makes an ambitious or greedy move while leaving their own queen en prise or ignoring an immediate tactical threat that wins their queen.

1956.label: Player makes a natural developing move in the opening while completely overlooking an elementary one-move capture of an undefended enemy piece (bishop, queen, or pawn).

1942.label: Players choose superficially attractive forcing moves (checks, double attacks, pawn grabs, captures for tempo) that backfire, missing quieter but objectively superior alternatives.

1953.label: Queen captures a seemingly undefended b-file pawn (the 'poisoned pawn'), venturing deep into enemy territory where it becomes trapped or loses critical tempo.

1944.label: Player makes greedy or flashy captures and forcing moves that leave their own pieces undefended, when a quieter preparatory move was required to maintain the advantage.

1949.label: Player moves their King instead of capturing an undefended or hanging major piece that would win decisive material immediately.

1947.label: Player grabs immediately available material or makes the obvious capture/move while missing a stronger intermediate move that would secure a much larger advantage or avoid disaster.

1952.label: Player reflexively captures an available enemy piece (usually a bishop) instead of finding the stronger tactical, defensive, or positional move that the position demands.

1948.label: In rook endgames, the player passively blockades passed pawns or makes aimless king moves instead of maintaining rook activity and distance, often allowing fatal exchanges or mating patterns.

1957.label: Player made slow, non-forcing moves (pawn pushes, rook lifts, castling) while the position demanded an immediate tactical capture or forcing response to neutralize or exploit a concrete threat.

1958.label: Player trades or hangs their sole remaining minor piece (usually a bishop) in an endgame, entering a hopeless pawn ending or losing critical defensive resources, when preserving the piece was essential.

1955.label: Players chose flashy checks or obvious captures over objectively stronger tactical moves that would have maintained or increased a decisive advantage.

1959.label: Player moves a piece (typically bishop or queen) to a square where it is immediately capturable by the opponent, hanging material in an attempt to attack or reposition.

1960.label: Player makes a slow pawn push or speculative move instead of the necessary piece exchange (usually rook trade) that would neutralize the opponent's tactical threats.

1961.label: Player repeatedly avoided winning or saving queen trades that would simplify into favorable or survivable endgames, instead making aggressive queen moves that hung material or allowed devastating tactics.

1968.label: King moves that abandon or fail to seize the opposition in pawn endgames, allowing the opponent's king to advance decisively.

1973.label: Player consistently fails to play the move threatening Qg7 checkmate (typically Qh6, Qf6, or Bf6), instead making passive or irrelevant moves that squander forced mating attacks.

1965.label: Player avoids the correct piece exchange (typically a bishop capture) in favor of passive repositioning moves, leaving pieces vulnerable to trapping or tactical exploitation.

1963.label: Player makes an impulsive capture (or pointless check) that appears to win material but leaves their own piece hanging or fatally weakens their position.

1962.label: Player has a concrete material-winning tactical blow available but plays a slow, non-forcing, or superficially aggressive move instead of converting the advantage.

1967.label: Player greedily promotes pawns or captures material immediately instead of playing a necessary preparatory or forcing intermediate move that would have yielded a far superior outcome.

1969.label: Player overlooks a simple capture of the opponent's undefended or hanging queen, instead playing a move with a different (often flashy or defensive) intent.

1964.label: Player greedily captures material (usually with the queen) while ignoring a devastating bishop sacrifice check that exploits the newly exposed king or undefended queen.

1976.label: Player consistently missed a devastating Qh5+ (or Qh4+) queen check exploiting the absence of the f-pawn to win material by force on the weakened king diagonal.

1966.label: Player makes aggressive or impatient moves (pawn advances, greedy captures, king marches) in endgames where quiet defensive positioning was required to hold the position.

1979.label: Player makes passive or slow moves while missing an immediately available capture of a hanging or undefended piece (typically a bishop on d6 or a critical pawn/piece that could be taken for free).

1980.label: Player fails to play the thematic Bxc3+ capture (resolving tension and damaging White's structure), instead leaving the bishop on a vulnerable square where it gets trapped or forked.

1971.label: Player grabs immediately available material (pawn or piece capture) instead of executing a superior tactical sequence that would yield a greater advantage.

1982.label: Routine castling that ignores an immediate tactical obligation, leaving a piece hanging or allowing a forced combination that the player should have addressed first.

1972.label: Player pushes a pawn to chase an aggressively-placed enemy piece, failing to see it can leap forward with a devastating fork or check instead of retreating.

1970.label: Player makes active-looking moves (rook lifts, piece advances, pawn pushes) while ignoring critical king safety crises that demand immediate defensive attention or simplification.

1974.label: Player consistently overlooks available forcing moves (checks, captures, sacrifices) that win material or deliver checkmate, instead choosing routine or passive alternatives.

1988.label: Player consistently missed the textbook Greek Gift sacrifice (Bxh7+/Bxh2+) that would have exposed the opponent's king to a winning attack.

1986.label: Player delivers a tempting but fruitless check (usually queen or bishop) instead of making a constructive developing move or capturing hanging material, gifting the opponent tempo and worsening their own position.

1978.label: Player fails to capture an available enemy queen (reducing lethal mating threats) and instead makes an irrelevant or greedy move, allowing forced checkmate.

1975.label: Player makes routine developing or positional pawn moves while an opponent's major piece (usually a queen) hangs undefended and available for immediate free capture.

1977.label: Player consistently chose immediately forcing moves (promotions, captures with check, spite checks) instead of quiet preparatory moves that addressed the actual critical positional need.

1981.label: Player moves their king (or ignores a threat) directly into an immediate checkmate or forced mate, when a desperate capture or interposition was the only survival move.

1992.label: Player consistently misses a knight capture on d5 (or similar central square) that wins material by simultaneously attacking the enemy queen, instead making passive or premature moves.

1985.label: Player avoids trading or sacrificing their queen/rook to enter a trivially winning pawn endgame, instead keeping pieces on with aimless checks or passive moves.

1997.label: Positions where the player missed an immediately decisive pawn advance (with check or forced promotion) in a won endgame, instead making a slower king move or non-forcing alternative.

1983.label: Player consistently misses simple queen captures of undefended pawns or pieces (especially Qxa7/Qxa2/Qxh7), choosing passive repositioning moves instead of taking free material.

1987.label: Player fails to blockade an enemy passed pawn by placing a piece directly on its promotion square or in its path, instead making irrelevant moves that allow the pawn to advance or promote.

1984.label: Player captures a piece for material gain while completely overlooking a devastating tactical threat (mate, fork, or discovered attack) that punishes the greedy capture.

1998.label: Player skips a forcing intermediate move with check (typically a bishop capture/sacrifice giving check) that would win material by deflecting the king before executing the main tactical idea.

1989.label: Player ignores a lethal queen-bishop battery along a long diagonal aimed at their king, missing the critical bishop interposition that blocks the mating threat.

1995.label: Player fails to execute a winning or equalizing rook capture/exchange that would eliminate the opponent's most dangerous attacking piece.

2001.label: Player gives a tempting but purposeless queen check that squanders a winning tactical opportunity, losing tempo and allowing the opponent to consolidate.

1991.label: In pawn/minor piece endgames, the player moves the king toward a peripheral pawn or retreats a piece passively instead of centralizing the king to control critical squares.

1994.label: Player makes slow or passive moves instead of executing a concrete Nxe6 knight capture that wins material and shatters the opponent's pawn structure.

1993.label: Player makes an ambitious or irrelevant move while ignoring an immediate tactical threat to their own undefended piece, when a simple defensive/developing move would solve the crisis.

1990.label: Player makes slow developing or positional moves, missing available pawn thrusts or captures that win material through forks or attacks on undefended pieces.

1996.label: Player makes a plausible-looking move (king walk, pawn push, or check) while completely overlooking that it leaves one of their own pieces undefended and capturable.

1999.label: In queen-vs-pawn endgames, the player moves the king directly behind or adjacent to their passed pawn to support promotion instead of maintaining king flexibility, activity, or stalemate resources on a more distant square.

2002.label: Player captures a piece prematurely, releasing positional or tactical tension, when a non-capturing move maintaining pressure or building the attack was far stronger.

2004.label: Player ignores a hanging or intruding enemy piece (usually a bishop on c3/c6) that can be trivially captured by a pawn, instead making a developing or active move that leaves the free material on the board.

2000.label: Player greedily captures material (pawn or minor piece) when they should first trade queens or eliminate the most dangerous attacking piece to neutralize threats.

2013.label: Player captures material with a rook (or other piece) while neglecting a fatal back-rank weakness, when the correct move was a quiet prophylactic (luft or king escape) to neutralize the checkmate threat.

2009.label: Player makes an ambitious move while completely overlooking that their own queen (or major piece) is left hanging or undefended, typically requiring a simple retreat or trade to save it.

2006.label: Player repeatedly overlooked a straightforward one-move capture that wins the opponent's queen or decisive material, instead playing inferior moves with other strategic intentions.

2003.label: Player grabs material or makes aggressive moves while their own king remains dangerously uncastled on an open file, allowing tactical refutations that win back more than was gained.

2010.label: Player chose a passive, reactive, or greedily materialistic move instead of the available forcing tactical continuation that would have been immediately decisive.

2007.label: Player moves a rook or pawn seeking activity while fatally abandoning the critical square or file defending their own king, allowing immediate tactical punishment.

2005.label: Player makes passive developing or retreating moves in the opening while missing time-sensitive captures (especially en passant) or forcing tactical shots that would have won material or seized the initiative.

2008.label: Player delivers a tempting check or aggressive capture that leaves their own piece hanging, when a quiet consolidating or defensive move was far superior.

2012.label: Player moves their bishop to an aggressively-placed but undefended square where it is immediately captured for free by an opponent's piece or pawn.

2011.label: Player moves a piece aggressively (usually attacking the opponent's queen) but the moved piece physically blocks or removes a critical defensive connection, leaving their own piece hanging.

2020.label: Player delivers a tempting but pointless queen check to the h-file, which is easily blocked or captured, wasting tempo and often hanging the queen or another piece.

2025.label: Player moves a bishop (or makes a non-capturing move) while missing an immediately available capture of an undefended or hanging enemy piece, typically a knight or minor piece that could be taken for free.

2014.label: In pawn endgames, the player advances a pawn prematurely instead of using the king to invade and attack enemy pawns, converting winning positions into draws or losses.

2018.label: Player captures a high-value piece or makes a tempting trade that removes their own dynamic resources, simplifying into a strategically lost position or walking into a tactic.

2019.label: Player consistently fails to recognize or prevent an opponent's knight fork, ignoring prophylactic moves that challenge or displace the threatening knight.

2022.label: Player moves the queen (often to the very square the knight should occupy) while missing a devastating knight fork with check that would win decisive material.

2015.label: In won or drawn pawn endgames, the player moves their king to the wrong square, failing to optimally position it to support their own passed pawn's promotion or contest the opponent's pawn race.

2017.label: In won or critical endgame positions, the player advances a pawn passively instead of finding the winning active piece move (king march, fork, or direct attack).

2021.label: Player moves the king passively or to a worse square instead of making an available winning capture that solves the tactical problem.

2023.label: Player gives a tempting but counterproductive check (with bishop or rook) instead of directly addressing a critical passed pawn that requires immediate blockade or capture.

2016.label: Player consistently chooses passive, slow, or 'natural' moves in the opening, missing the one critical moment to strike with a concrete tactical or central blow that wins material or a decisive advantage.

2031.label: Player fails to control or blockade the opponent's pawn promotion square, allowing a decisive promotion that could have been prevented.

2035.label: Player consistently misses winning pawn or piece checks that deflect the opponent's king away from defending a key piece, allowing material gain.

2024.label: Player gives a rook check that feels aggressive but squanders a winning position by missing the immediately decisive tactical blow (promotion, sacrifice, or mate).

2036.label: Player misses a winning bishop capture along the long diagonal (Bxg7 or Bxg2) that wins material by exploiting an undefended pawn and exposed rook.

2030.label: Player overlooks that the opponent's queen is hanging and freely capturable, instead making a passive king move or grabbing lesser material.

2028.label: Player missed a winning or advantageous knight capture (usually Nxd4) that would exploit tactical vulnerabilities of a centralized enemy knight, instead choosing slow developing or prophylactic moves.

2034.label: Player reflexively trades queens with check instead of maintaining the queen to exploit the opponent's vulnerable king through forks, sacrifices, or sustained attacking pressure.

2026.label: Player overlooks a decisive forcing move (checkmate, sacrifice, or critical capture) and instead plays a passive or routine move that hangs material or walks into a mating attack.

2029.label: Player prematurely exchanges a dominant centralized knight via a forcing check or capture instead of maintaining it to build a lasting positional advantage.

2041.label: Positions where the player moves their king to an exposed square (or makes a passive move) instead of finding the critical tactical defense or counterattack that resolves the position.

2033.label: Player fails to capture an undefended central e-pawn with a knight in the opening, instead making a passive or slow developing move.

2032.label: Player captures a tempting pawn (often advanced/passed) while missing a superior move that wins a hanging piece or major material.

2027.label: Player captures or moves with the knight when a bishop or pawn capture was the correct recapture, leaving pieces hanging due to using the wrong attacking piece.

2037.label: Player gives a flashy check or fork that looks forcing but actually hangs their own piece or liquidates into a lost position, when a quiet non-checking move was far superior.

2039.label: Player greedily captures material with a pawn or minor piece while failing to notice their own queen is left undefended or fatally exposed to tactics.

2038.label: Player moves a piece to attack the opponent's queen while completely overlooking an immediate checkmate threat against their own king.

2040.label: Player trades queens into a lost endgame when keeping queens on the board (typically via perpetual check) would have maintained a draw.

2043.label: In endgames with advanced passed pawns, the player pushes the pawn one rank closer to promotion instead of first activating or repositioning the king to support it.

2044.label: Player ignores an enemy passed pawn on the verge of promotion instead of capturing it, allowing the pawn to queen or create decisive threats.

2042.label: Player ignores existential threats (enemy passed pawns about to promote or own hanging pieces) to play slow, irrelevant pawn pushes or king moves instead of the required defensive capture.

2045.label: Player ignores a simple winning capture of a hanging or inadequately defended piece in favor of a slow positional or pawn-advancing move in the endgame.

2047.label: Player chose a passive or repositioning move instead of a forcing capture with check (usually a queen capture) that would have won material, delivered checkmate, or secured a draw through perpetual.

2046.label: Player moved the king passively when a forcing tactic (capture, check, or fork) would have won decisive material or delivered checkmate.
